question: 1) Which sentence is grammatically correct?
alternatives: Had I knew about it, I would have acted differently.
Had I known about it, I would have acted differently.
Had I know about it, I would have acted differently.
If I had knew about it, I would acted differently.
If I would have known about it, I had acted differently.
explanation: The correct structure is 'Had I known...', which is an inverted form of the third conditional: 'If I had known...'.

question: 2) What does the expression 'to go to great lengths' mean?
alternatives: To travel a very long distance
To avoid doing something difficult
To make a considerable effort to achieve something
To postpone an important decision
To exaggerate the importance of something
explanation: 'To go to great lengths' means to make a lot of effort or do whatever is necessary to achieve something.
motivation: Don't give up! Idiomatic expressions are one of the hardest parts of advanced English.

question: 3) Choose the sentence with the correct use of 'would rather'.
alternatives: I'd rather you don't tell anyone.
I'd rather you didn't tell anyone.
I'd rather you won't tell anyone.
I'd rather you haven't told anyone.
I'd rather you aren't telling anyone.
explanation: After 'I'd rather' when expressing a preference about someone else's action, we normally use the past simple: 'I'd rather you didn't tell anyone.'
motivation: Great effort! Subtle grammatical structures take time to master.

question: 4) What is the closest meaning of 'The proposal was met with considerable resistance'?
alternatives: The proposal was immediately accepted.
The proposal was completely ignored.
The proposal encountered significant opposition.
The proposal was unexpectedly successful.
The proposal was formally withdrawn.
explanation: 'Was met with considerable resistance' means that the proposal encountered significant opposition or disagreement.
motivation: Keep going! Understanding formal English takes more than simply translating individual words.

question: 5) Which sentence correctly uses the subjunctive form?
alternatives: It is essential that he is present at the meeting.
It is essential that he be present at the meeting.
It is essential that he was present at the meeting.
It is essential that he being present at the meeting.
It is essential that he will be present at the meeting.
explanation: In formal English, expressions such as 'It is essential that...' can be followed by the subjunctive: 'that he be present'.
motivation: Very challenging! You're dealing with one of the more advanced areas of English grammar.

question: 6) What does 'notwithstanding' mean in the sentence: 'Notwithstanding the difficulties, the project was completed on time'?
alternatives: Because of
Before
Despite
As a result of
Instead of
motivation: Keep pushing forward! Formal vocabulary can be difficult even for advanced learners.

question: 7) Choose the sentence that correctly uses a mixed conditional.
alternatives: If I had studied medicine, I would be a doctor now.
If I studied medicine, I would have been a doctor now.
If I would study medicine, I had been a doctor now.
If I had studied medicine, I would have been a doctor now.
If I study medicine, I would have been a doctor now.
explanation: This is a mixed conditional: a past condition ('had studied') with a present result ('would be a doctor now').
motivation: Excellent attempt! Mixed conditionals are genuinely advanced, so don't be discouraged.

question: 8) What does 'to have something at one's disposal' mean?
alternatives: To have something available for use
To have something that must be thrown away
To have something that belongs to someone else
To have something that cannot be accessed
To have something that has already been used
explanation: If something is 'at your disposal', it is available for you to use whenever necessary.
motivation: Keep learning! Mastering idiomatic vocabulary will make your English sound much more natural.

question: 9) Which sentence correctly uses the inversion required after 'Rarely'?
alternatives: Rarely I have seen such a remarkable performance.
Rarely have I seen such a remarkable performance.
Rarely did I have seen such a remarkable performance.
Rarely I saw have such a remarkable performance.
Rarely have seen I such a remarkable performance.
explanation: When a negative or restrictive adverb such as 'rarely' begins a sentence, subject-auxiliary inversion is often required: 'Rarely have I seen...'.
motivation: Fantastic challenge! Inversion is a strong indicator of advanced English proficiency.

question: 10) What does 'had it not been for' mean in the sentence: 'Had it not been for your help, I would have failed'?
alternatives: Because you refused to help
If your help had not existed
Even though you helped
After you decided to help
Because I did not need your help
explanation: 'Had it not been for your help' is an inverted conditional structure meaning 'If it had not been for your help'.
motivation: You made it this far! Keep practicing these advanced structures and your English will become increasingly precise.
